title: They Called His Partition Film Anti-National. Imtiaz Ali's Response Was the Sharpest Thing Bollywood Has Said All Year.
excerpt: Main Vaapas Aaunga showed Pakistan without terrorists. The trolls came. A.R. Rahman posted a laughing emoji. Then the director said what nobody in the industry will say about Indian Muslim patriotism.
body:
Here's the scene: a Partition-era love story opens to a whisper at the box office, battles the kind of indifference that usually buries Indian films before their first Monday, and then does something nobody expected — it recovers. Not because of a marketing stunt or a celebrity endorsement, but because people walked out of theatres genuinely moved. **Main Vaapas Aaunga**, Imtiaz Ali's reunion with **Diljit Dosanjh** after the devastating *Amar Singh Chamkila*, is a quiet film about a loud wound. And the internet cannot handle it.

<youtube>https://youtube.com/watch?v=PRUTWluKRW8</youtube>

The sin? Showing Pakistan as a country where people live. Not as a breeding ground for terrorists. Not as a shadowy threat across the border. Just — a place. With streets and families and chai and loss. In the film, set against the backdrop of undivided India, **Vedang Raina** plays the younger version of **Naseeruddin Shah's** character, a man still haunted by the land he left behind in 1947. **Sharvari** plays the woman at the centre of that longing. The story doesn't pick sides. It picks people.

That was enough to earn *Main Vaapas Aaunga* the "anti-national" tag from social media's most predictable corner. The accusation was simple and absurd: showing Pakistan without spies or terrorists was apparently an act of betrayal.

## A.R. Rahman's One-Emoji Response

**A.R. Rahman**, who composed the film's score alongside longtime collaborator **Irshad Kamil**, responded first — and in the most A.R. Rahman way possible. Someone posted a satirical Instagram slide mocking the backlash: "Anti-National? Movie Dares To Show Pakistan Without Terrorists and Secret Agents." Rahman shared it to his story with a single laughing-with-tears emoji. No statement. No thread. Just one emoji that said more than a press release ever could.

But it was Imtiaz Ali who delivered the line that has since cut through the noise. Speaking to *The Tribune* this week, the director said something that Bollywood directors almost never say out loud:

> "More than anyone else, Indian Muslims have proved their patriotism by deciding to stay in India when they had a choice." — Imtiaz Ali

In an industry that has spent the last several years carefully sidestepping anything that could trigger a boycott hashtag, an established filmmaker looked directly at the camera and said the thing. He didn't qualify it. He didn't couch it in apology. He just said it.

## No Agenda, No Apology

Ali also pushed back against the idea that his film carries any political agenda. "The film is set in undivided India, so it's not about loving or hating Pakistan," he told the paper. "Besides, of all the people I met, none of them spoke of hatred." When asked about the film's central refrain — that home is where the heart is — he offered something unexpectedly personal:

> "Home is a version of who you were. Like Ishar in Main Vaapas Aaunga... we all yearn to return to being that person we were when we were home." — Imtiaz Ali

If you're part of the diaspora, that line doesn't need an explainer. It's the feeling of your parents' kitchen. The house they sold before they moved. The city you left and the version of yourself you left in it.

## The Box Office Climbed When Nobody Was Looking

The film opened to a subdued ₹1.15 crore on its first day — the kind of number that usually triggers the "flop" headlines before Friday night. But something unusual happened. Word-of-mouth did what trailers couldn't. Day two climbed to ₹1.85 crore. Day three hit ₹2.50 crore. By its sixth day, *Main Vaapas Aaunga* had crossed ₹10 crore domestically, never once dipping below its opening-day number. In an era where most Bollywood films collapse by Monday, this one kept rising.

The music has been a significant driver. The **Imtiaz Ali–A.R. Rahman–Irshad Kamil** partnership is arguably the most celebrated creative trio in modern Bollywood music, responsible for the soundtracks of *Rockstar*, *Highway*, *Tamasha*, and *Amar Singh Chamkila*. Their latest work has been called one of the strongest Hindi film albums of the year.

## What It Means

*Main Vaapas Aaunga* isn't the kind of film that trends because of a dance number or a fight sequence. It trends because it makes people uncomfortable in exactly the right way. A Partition story that refuses to draw villains. A director who refuses to apologise for nuance. A composer who responds to manufactured outrage with a laughing emoji.

In 2026 Bollywood, that's not just rare. It's radical.
